messages.subject: Re: [SOCIAL NETWORK] [Rqtl2-disc] Zooming in on plot_coefCC
messages.body_plain:

messages.subject: Re: [SOCIAL NETWORK] [Rqtl2-disc] Zooming in on plot_coefCC
messages.body_plain:
The problem is like that if you use options that create multiple panels, they're using the equivalent of mfrow to create the layout, and you can't nest two of those.

For example, if you want coefficients and lod curves, it'll pass you to plot_coef_and_lod(), which uses layout(), which is a fancier version of par(mfrow).

https://github.com/rqtl/qtl2/blob/main/R/plot_coef_and_lod.R#L44

So I think you're stuck using the small pieces and assembling them yourself.

karl

messages.subject: DO cross questions
messages.body_plain:
We are looking for genetic modifiers of a gene knockout. The gene KO is on the X chromosome. We already know that KO/X[C57BL6/J] x males from 8 founder strains of DO yields F1 with heritable phenotypic variation. Now we are doing the DO cross to map the modifiers. Here is our current cross strategy: KO/X[C57BL6/J] x DO male -> F1 KO male. Genotype and phenotype the F1 males.

Questions:
- In R/qtl2, what is the correct cross_type, and what should the cross_info file look like
- If we take the F1 KO/X females and cross to DO male, will this increase the statistical power or information yield of the cross? Could the data from the F1 cross and F2 cross be integrated in the same analysis?

Thank you.

messages.body_plain: A quantitative trait that we are analyzing is not normally distributed. How to deal with this in the R/qtl2 analysis? The trait is treadmill endurance. In our study, mutant mice have low treadmill endurance, but normal mice have endurance that exceeds the length of the study (ie they saturate the assay). While this could be coded as a binary trait, that would lose the quantification of the phenotype in mutants, which varies considerably between mutants on different genetic backgrounds.

messages.subject: Re: DO cross questions
messages.body_plain:
You can use the cross type "dof1". There is some discussion of the input file information required at the following

    https://kbroman.org/qtl2/assets/vignettes/input_files.html#DOF1

The basic thing is that the parental genotype data needs 8 strains: the 8 DO founders, and then the strain the DO mice were crossed to. So C57BL6/J, repeated.

Regarding your idea of crossing pairs of these (KO x DO)F1 mice to make an F2, I think I would prefer to see many more (KO x DO)F1. Ultimately, you'll be as interested in mapping precision as in power, and getting additional F1s will provide more information in that regard.

cheers,
karl

messages.subject: Re: Phenotype that is not normally distributed
messages.subject_clean: Phenotype that is not normally distributed
messages.body_plain:
Our main strategies for dealing with non-normal traits are:

  - transform the phenotype (for example, take log or square-root)
  - use a robust method, such as rank-based. Related to that is to convert the phenotypes to ranks and then to normal quantiles, as with the nqrank function in the R/qtl1 package (qtl::nqrank)
  - use a method that is tailored to the specific phenotype distribution, such as with a generalized linear model. This isn't implemented within R/qtl2, but you could use the results of calc_genoprob() and do this on your own. If you need to get linear mixed models in there too, it starts to get really hard.

karl

messages.subject: Re: DO cross questions
messages.body_plain:
I feel like the F2 individuals are equally or maybe less informative than the F1 individuals.
For power to detect a QTL, they are about equal, provided that the F2 cross is not just a few large sibships.

More importantly, for precision of mapping a QTL: the problem with the F2, is that they will be in sibships. Most of the mapping precision is coming from the recombination events on the DO chromosome, which accumulated over the many generations of the DO. But in the F2 mice, you’ll be seeing pieces of the same set of DO chromosomes repeatedly, and so the same historical recombination events repeated, whereas if you had a set of independent F1 mice, each would have different, independent sets of recombination events.

karl

messages.subject_clean: Phenotype that is not normally distributed
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I'm trying to build my understanding of the significance of assumptions about normality in relation to the statistical models in qtl2, and I noticed a focus in this thread on the normal distribution of the trait itself, as opposed to normal distribution of the residuals of that trait. Is there a significance to the normality of the simple trait distribution that is good to understand here (beyond just questions of "are there concerning outliers in this data?"), or is this thread really concerned with normal distribution of the residuals, though not explicitly stated?
I'd appreciate anyone's input here.
-Mark Sfeir

On Thursday, September 8, 2022 at 10:39:51 AM UTC-4 kbr...@gmail.com wrote:
> Our main strategies for dealing with non-normal traits are:
>
>   - transform the phenotype (for example, take log or square-root)
>   - use a robust method, such as rank-based. Related to that is to convert the phenotypes to ranks and then to normal quantiles, as with the nqrank function in the R/qtl1 package (qtl::nqrank)
>   - use a method that is tailored to the specific phenotype distribution, such as with a generalized linear model. This isn't implemented within R/qtl2, but you could use the results of calc_genoprob() and do this on your own. If you need to get linear mixed models in there too, it starts to get really hard.
>
> karl
>
> On Thursday, September 8, 2022 at 7:12:28 AM UTC-5 w...@pulab.org wrote:
> > A quantitative trait that we are analyzing is not normally distributed. How to deal with this in the R/qtl2 analysis? The trait is treadmill endurance. In our study, mutant mice have low treadmill endurance, but normal mice have endurance that exceeds the length of the study (ie they saturate the assay). While this could be coded as a binary trait, that would lose the quantification of the phenotype in mutants, which varies considerably between mutants on different genetic backgrounds.

messages.subject: RE: [SOCIAL NETWORK] [Rqtl2-disc] Re: Phenotype that is not normally distributed
messages.subject_clean: [SOCIAL NETWORK] [Rqtl2-disc] Re: Phenotype that is not normally distributed
messages.body_plain:
It’s true, in a linear models course, one of the assumptions is that the residuals are normally distributed. I think that, in practice, having your response be normally distributed, as opposed to log-normal or something really skewed, helps to produce normally distributed residuals. It doesn’t guarantee it. But we can’t do the usual model diagnostics at each marker in a QTL mapping study. So it’s a pragmatic way of trying to satisfy the linear model assumptions.

I don’t have any examples handy, but I have seen QTL get stronger when the phenotype was standardized.  And I’ve seen spurious QTL disappear once the phenotype was transformed to make it more normally distributed.

Dan

messages.subject: Re: DO cross questions
messages.body_plain:
I've looked more closely at the two main genotype diagnostic functions for the DOF1:

 - calc_errorlod() is behaving correctly, I believe
 - predict_snpgeno() is messed up, but I have a quick fix

With your DOF1 data, it _does_ seem like the genotyping error rate is 30%, but there's something weird going on, because it's like half the markers have no errors and half of the markers have an error rates >20%.

karl

On Friday, September 23, 2022 at 2:21:41 PM UTC-5 Karl Broman wrote:
> It seems like neither calc_errorlod() not predict_snpgeno() are working for DOF1 data. The structure of the DOF1 is completely different than all of the other kinds of multi-parent populations, and I don't think I paid proper attention to that.
